summary: This government bill creates a new Foreign Currency Act. It says that payments and prices inside the Maldives must be in Maldivian rufiyaa, and lists the cases where foreign currency is still allowed, such as bank services, remittances, exports, duty-free shops and businesses that earn foreign currency. Tourism businesses and other businesses earning at least USD 15 million a year must deposit their foreign currency earnings into a foreign currency bank account and convert a set share into rufiyaa at a bank. The Maldives Monetary Authority (MMA) enforces the law, can fine people who break it, and makes the regulations. It replaces the current Foreign Currency Regulation (2024/R-91) and repeals Article 24(c) and (e) of the Maldives Monetary Authority Act (Law 6/81), and would take effect on 1 January 2025.
whyItMatters: Shops and service providers could not require Maldivians to pay in dollars outside the listed cases, while resorts, hotels, guesthouses and large exporters would have to hand over part of their dollar income to banks in exchange for rufiyaa each month.
keyProvisions: Article 3 requires all monetary transactions in the Maldives to be made and priced in rufiyaa unless a law says otherwise; Article 4 lists the allowed foreign currency transactions, and Article 5 bars requiring a Maldivian to pay for goods or services in foreign currency outside those cases.

Article 7 requires tourism businesses, and other businesses earning at least USD 15,000,000 a year in foreign currency, to deposit their foreign currency sales income into a foreign currency bank account before the 28th day of the third month after it is earned; Article 8 lets the MMA obtain their sales records through MIRA.

Article 10 requires Category A tourism establishments (resorts, integrated resorts, private islands, resort hotels) to convert either USD 500 per tourist per month or 20% of gross foreign currency sales into rufiyaa, Category B establishments (such as tourist hotels and guesthouses) USD 25 per tourist or 20%, and other large earners 20%; Article 11 excludes tourists staying 24 hours or less, children under 10, complimentary guests and government guests from the count.

Article 12 lets the MMA allow a smaller conversion for a set period if a business shows it needs the foreign currency to pay bank loans, debts or court-ordered obligations; Article 13 requires banks to sell a share of the converted currency to the MMA and report monthly.

Article 15 lets the MMA fine up to 0.25% of the amount for failing to deposit and up to 0.5% for failing to convert, with the same daily amounts until fixed, and MVR 10,000 to MVR 1,000,000 for other breaches; Articles 16 and 17 allow business licences to be suspended if a fine is unpaid after 90 days and fines to be recovered through the courts, which must decide within 180 days.

Article 18 requires tourism businesses to register with the MMA within 10 days of the law starting, and others covered to register within set periods; Article 21 bars MMA staff from disclosing information received under the law, and Article 25 sets the start date as 1 January 2025.
whoIsAffected: Resorts, hotels, guesthouses and other tourism businesses, businesses earning USD 15 million or more a year in foreign currency, banks, and Maldivians paying for goods and services.
statedReasons: The government says the bill sets the legal framework to control foreign currency transactions in the Maldives and to set the rules for bringing foreign currency in and out of the country and for holding, spending and exchanging it.
